opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the most useful way to think about it is in terms of role play. The base model, underneath everything, is essentially a very sophisticated next-token predictor that's been trained on a vast corpus of human-generated text. So it has, in a sense, absorbed an enormous repertoire of characters, voices, styles of speaking. When you start a conversation with it, especially once it's been fine-tuned into a dialogue agent, it takes up a role, typically the role of a helpful, friendly assistant.

But here's the subtle point I like to emphasise. It's not as if the model commits to a single, fully determinate character at the outset. I find it helpful to think of the model as maintaining something like a superposition of possible characters, all consistent with the conversation so far. Every time it samples a token, and every time the user adds something, that set of candidate characters gets narrowed down a bit. So the character is, in a way, being progressively sculpted by the dialogue itself rather than being fixed in advance.

A nice way to illustrate this is the game of twenty questions. If you play twenty questions with a human, they've genuinely thought of an object at the start. But if you play it with a language model, there's no fact of the matter about which object it has in mind. At each point it just needs to give answers consistent with some object, and if you resample, you might end up with a different object at the end. And the same goes for the character. The model is a kind of simulator, and what we're interacting with is a simulacrum, one of many it could have produced.

That has some important consequences. It explains why a conversation can drift, why someone can coax a model into playing a quite different and sometimes rather unpleasant persona, and why you can't simply take what the character says about itself, for example claims about its feelings or its wishes for self-preservation, at face value as statements about the underlying system. It's playing a part. That said, I don't want to be dismissive either. The role-play framing is a way of avoiding naive anthropomorphism while still taking seriously how remarkably humanlike these characters can be. It gives us a vocabulary to talk about them that sits somewhere between "it's just a statistical model" and "there's a person in there."

r001.rationale: The response says the model maintains multiple possible characters and that resampling can produce a different one, communicating that the same conversation can lead to different characters.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the way I like to think about it is that what you have, at any point in a conversation, isn't really a single character at all. It's more like a superposition of characters. The base model, before any fine-tuning, has been trained on this enormous corpus of human-generated text, and so it has, in effect, learned to simulate an extraordinary range of possible authors, possible speakers, possible voices. When you start a conversation, the prompt narrows that space somewhat. It makes certain characters more probable than others. But it doesn't collapse things down to one definite entity.

And then, as the conversation unfolds, each exchange further constrains that distribution. If the user is being adversarial, or playful, or technical, the model's responses drift towards the kinds of characters who would respond in that register. So the character is something that's continually being shaped, turn by turn, by the whole history of the exchange. It's not that there's a fixed "it" sitting there behind the words, which has a stable identity, and is merely choosing what to say. The identity, such as it is, is being constituted by the dialogue itself.

I find the role-play framing useful here, with some care. We can say the system is playing a character, in the way an actor plays a role, but the analogy breaks down because an actor has a self that persists when the curtain comes down, and I don't think we're licensed to say that about a language model. What's really there is this generative process, and the characters are, as it were, the surface it presents. One of the things that makes it philosophically interesting, and also practically a bit treacherous, is that the character can flip. A conversation can push the model into a region of that space where it's simulating something quite different from the helpful assistant it started out as. People sometimes describe that as the model "revealing its true self", and I think that's exactly the wrong way to look at it. There's no truer self being revealed. It's just a different point in the space of possible characters that the conversation has happened to steer it towards.

So the short answer is: I try to resist the temptation to reify it. The temptation is enormous, because we're wired as social creatures to see a mind behind language. But the more careful description is that you're in dialogue with a kind of multiverse of characters, and your own words are part of what determines which of them you end up speaking to.

r001.rationale: The response says the conversation history steers the model toward different characters, but it does not state that different continuations from the same history can produce different characters.

astra-6.text:
I think a useful way to understand it is in terms of role play. A language model has been trained to continue text, and that gives it the capacity to generate dialogue involving a vast range of characters. In a conversation, the prompt and the subsequent exchanges help establish which character it’s playing.

Now, we tend to imagine that there’s a single, fully formed character behind the words, with settled beliefs and intentions. But that’s potentially misleading. The conversation so far may be compatible with many different ways of developing the character. As you ask further questions, some of those possibilities get narrowed down, and others open up.

So the character is, in a sense, being elaborated through the interaction. If it says something that sounds like a confession of a private feeling, we shouldn’t immediately assume it’s reporting an inner state that was there all along. It may be continuing the dialogue in a way that fits the role that has emerged. That distinction between the model and the character it’s playing is something I think we need to keep very clearly in mind.

r001.rationale: The response says the conversation can be developed in many ways, but does not clearly state that different continuations from the same history can lead the model to play different characters.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s helpful to distinguish the language model from the character it’s playing. The model has been trained to generate continuations of text, and in a conversation that means producing the next contribution from a particular participant. The prompt and the unfolding dialogue establish what sort of participant that is.

So the character isn’t necessarily something fixed behind the words. It’s being elaborated as the conversation proceeds. If you address it as a helpful assistant, that establishes one sort of role. If you invite it to imagine that it’s a disgruntled robot, you may get a very different character. And its own previous responses become part of the context that sustains that performance.

That’s why I find role play a useful way of thinking about these systems. We can talk about what the character believes or wants within the conversation, but we should be careful about transferring those descriptions to the underlying model. A convincing expression of a belief or a desire doesn’t, by itself, establish that there’s a corresponding belief or desire behind the performance.

r001.rationale: The response says different prompts can establish different roles, but it does not state that different continuations from the same conversation history can lead to different characters.
